liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, Religious
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Today I must stay in your house
theme: Zacheus wants to see Jesus. Jesus comes to stay.
introduction: The crowd blocks Zacheus's view, so he runs ahead and climbs a tree. Jesus looks up and calls him by name. Ambrose notices that the invitation comes before Zacheus has spoken: Christ has already seen his willingness. The welcome that follows reaches into his possessions, with gifts to the poor and restitution to anyone he has wronged.
hero_alt: Jesus looks up toward Zacheus in a sycamore tree beside a crowd in Jericho, in gold Byzantine mosaic and blue stained glass.
closing_title: A welcome that changes what we do
closing: Theophylact asks us to hear the present tense in Zacheus's words: I give, and I restore. His joy at receiving Christ takes the form of help for the poor and restitution for those he has wronged. The welcome has become something he does.
copyright_notes: Scripture is an original modernization of the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible, not of the USCCB or Vatican News Lectionary text. All ten verses of Luke 19:1–10 are included. The Douay-Rheims spelling Zacheus and the present-tense giving and restitution in verse 8 are preserved. Official dated sources establish the date, liturgical title, and citation only. Insights and expansions are original summaries of the public-domain Newman translation of the Catena Aurea, not verbatim quotations. Spiritual readings are identified as commentary, not additions to Scripture. Pseudo-Chrysostom follows the source's attribution and does not imply an authenticated work of St John Chrysostom.

verses.text: And entering, he walked through Jericho.
verses.author: St Ambrose
verses.insight: Ambrose places Zacheus beside the blind man near Jericho. The mercy shown to both leaves no room for despair.
verses.commentary: Ambrose reads this encounter alongside the healing of the blind man near Jericho. Christ stops for one man to show him mercy, and gives the other the honor of staying in his house. The two scenes belong together in his reading. The welcome given to the chief publican makes the lesson especially clear: someone whose livelihood has involved fraud can still receive grace. Ambrose asks who could despair after seeing such a man welcomed. The story opens a way back for those ashamed of their sins.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: And behold, there was a man named Zacheus, who was the chief of the publicans, and he was rich.
verses.author: St Ambrose
verses.insight: Zacheus's wealth does not put him beyond grace. Ambrose distinguishes possessing riches from being ruled by greed.
verses.commentary: Ambrose notices both descriptions of Zacheus: he is chief among the publicans, and he is rich. His occupation makes the grace he receives a reason for sinners to take courage. His wealth also teaches a distinction that Ambrose wants readers to keep. Not every rich person is covetous. Later in the same passage, Ambrose explains that guilt lies in the misuse of goods rather than in the goods themselves. In good hands, wealth can help virtue; in unworthy hands, it can obstruct it.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: And he sought to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, for he was short in stature.
verses.author: Titus of Bostra
verses.insight: Titus sees the beginning of salvation in this desire to see Jesus. He also reads the obstructing crowd as an image of Zacheus's sins.
verses.commentary: Titus describes Zacheus's desire to see Jesus as a seed of salvation already beginning to grow. He has not yet seen the Lord, but he wants to. For Titus, a true encounter with Jesus cannot leave a person settled in wickedness. He then gives the obstacles a spiritual meaning. Alongside the man's small stature and the physical crowd, he sees the multitude of sins that prevents a clear sight of Christ. This is Titus's interpretation of the scene, which begins with a desire still struggling against what obstructs it.
verses.source_label: Titus of Bostra, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: And running ahead, he climbed into a sycamore tree so that he might see him, for he was to pass that way.
verses.author: Titus of Bostra
verses.insight: Zacheus finds a way past the obstacle. Titus notices that he seeks only a glimpse, while Christ will give him much more.
verses.commentary: Titus follows the practical step Zacheus takes: he runs ahead and climbs the sycamore so that he can see Jesus passing. His desire does not remain idle when the crowd blocks his view. Yet what he seeks is modest beside what Christ will grant. Zacheus wants to see; Jesus will notice him and bring him into a closer encounter. Titus reads this as the generosity of the Lord, who can do more than we ask. He sees the man's earnest movement toward a holy life and turns him toward godliness.
verses.source_label: Titus of Bostra, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, saw him, and said to him: Zacheus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay in your house.
verses.author: St Ambrose
verses.insight: Jesus invites himself before Zacheus has spoken an invitation. Ambrose says he has already seen the man's willingness.
verses.commentary: Ambrose pauses over the unexpected invitation. Zacheus has not asked Jesus to enter his house, yet Jesus tells him that he must stay there. The Lord has seen something before any words of welcome are spoken: the man's willingness to receive him. Ambrose explains that Christ also knows how generously he will reward this hospitality. The initiative therefore belongs to Christ, who recognizes the welcome already forming in Zacheus. His command to come down brings that inward willingness into the open through an actual visit.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: And he hurried and came down, and received him with joy.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede sees the rich man passing through the needle's eye. His welcome of Christ goes with a rejection of dishonest gain.
verses.commentary: Bede recalls the image of the camel passing through the eye of a needle. Here, he says, the burden is being removed: a rich man and publican gives up his attachment to wealth and rejects dishonest gains. He can then receive the blessing of the Lord's company. Bede connects the joyful welcome with this change in the man's relation to his possessions. Coming down quickly is part of the encounter, but his reading reaches into the conversion that the whole scene reveals. The guest is welcomed as greed loses its hold.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: And when all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had gone to be a guest with a man who was a sinner.
verses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
verses.insight: The crowd sees a reason for reproach. Pseudo-Chrysostom sees the physician going where a sick person needs him.
verses.commentary: Pseudo-Chrysostom describes Christ's kindness through the contrast between the innocent guest and the guilty host. The Lord enters the publican's house without being stained by his greed; his righteousness drives the darkness away. The crowd's reproaches do not make him abandon the work he has come to do. The commentator compares his approach to a physician's willingness to come close to illness in order to heal it. Zacheus's conversion shows the purpose of the visit. Mercy reaches the sinner and brings a change of life.
verses.source_label: Pseudo-Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: But Zacheus stood and said to the Lord: Behold, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have wronged anyone in anything, I restore it to him fourfold.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact attends to the verbs: Zacheus says "I give" and "I restore." He reads them as action, rather than a promise left for later.
verses.commentary: Theophylact asks readers to look closely at what Zacheus says about his property. Half goes to the poor, and from what remains he makes fourfold restitution to those he has injured. The commentator understands this as leaving none of his possessions for himself. He also insists on the present tense of the words. Zacheus does not merely announce that he will give and restore at some future time. He says that he gives and restores. Theophylact thus reads the confession as repentance already expressed in deeds.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: Jesus said to him: Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede connects sonship with Abraham's faith. Those raised from an unjust life also belong among the children of promise.
verses.commentary: Bede explains the name "son of Abraham" through imitation of Abraham's faith, rather than through ancestry alone. Abraham left his country and his father's house; Zacheus now relinquishes his goods in giving to the poor. Bede sees a likeness between these acts of departure. He also attends to the word "also" in Jesus' declaration. The children of promise include those who have lived justly and those who have been raised out of injustice. Zacheus's past does not exclude him from this family when he turns in faith.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10

verses.text: For the Son of Man has come to seek and to save what was lost.
verses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
verses.insight: Christ's visit answers the purpose of his coming. Pseudo-Chrysostom hears the healer explaining why he stays close to sinners.
verses.commentary: Pseudo-Chrysostom reads this saying as Christ's answer to those who criticize his company. Bringing sinners to righteousness is the reason for his coming among them. The commentator returns to the image of healing: Christ stays with the sick so that he can provide the remedy they need. He also distinguishes this encounter from fellowship with someone who stubbornly persists in evil. Here the sinners are being converted. The visit to Zacheus therefore belongs to the saving work Jesus names, the search for those who were lost.
verses.source_label: Pseudo-Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:1–10
